Diabetes Complications and Annual Care

the annual care bundle and the outcome noun · kidney screening by detection threshold · foot ulcers read by exam, not risk profileIs the outcome morbidity, mortality, hospitalization or benefit, which test catches the reversible stage, and does the exam overrule the risk profile?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Read the outcome noun first: morbidity screen for a complication; mortality smoking cessation
  • Kidney screen: spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), the most sensitive test, at diagnosis in type 2, 5 years after it in type 1, then yearly
  • A painless, warm, plantar ulcer is neuropathic, but pulses and the ankle-brachial index (ABI) are still checked
What it is

Diabetes damages retina, kidney and nerve; retinopathy is the most common preventable complication; each can be silent until late

Driver

Glycation of small vessels and the glomerular basement membrane

Triggers

Diabetes duration (non-modifiable) and degree of hyperglycemia

Hypertension, smoking

Chain

Hyperfiltration albuminuria 30 to 300 mg/g overt proteinuria falling GFR

Neuropathy unfelt trauma at pressure points ulcer contiguous osteomyelitis Fiber typesSmall fibers: pain, burning, autonomic dysfunction (dry skin). Large fibers: sensory loss, which lets injury go unnoticed. It can be present when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed, and diabetes is the most common cause of neuropathic ulcers.

Insights

A normal creatinine does not exclude early kidney disease: hyperfiltration may keep it normal

The exam overrules the risk profile: a neuropathic ulcer still needs its perfusion checked PerfusionNeuropathy hides ischemic pain, and calcified vessels raise the ABI, so a normal index makes arterial disease less likely without excluding it.

3Differential
Leg and foot ulcers, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Neuropathic (diabetic) ulcerPainless, plantar over a metatarsal head or heel, callusWarm, dry foot; normal pulses; monofilament not felt
Arterial ulcerPainful toe tips or lateral malleolus, worse elevatedCool, hairless skin; absent pulses; ABI 0.9 or less
Venous stasis ulcerShallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolusHemosiderin, edema, normal pulses; duplex ultrasound
Charcot arthropathy (neuropathic joint)Weeks of a warm, swollen foot, no ulcer, no feverNeuropathy, normal labs; radiographs or MRI; casting
Pressure ulcerSacrum, heel or trochanter in an immobile patientStaged by depth
Pyoderma gangrenosumDays of rapid, very painful growth; violaceous undermined borderInflammatory bowel disease; biopsy and steroids, never debride
Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a scar)Over 3 months unhealed in a scar; rolled edgesBiopsy
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
"Prevent morbidity"Complications, disabilityScreen for one: the dilated eye exam
"Reduce mortality"DeathSmoking cessation
"Reduce hospitalization"AdmissionsTreat the driver of decompensation
"Most beneficial"Largest effect, any outcomeUsually smoking cessation
Total protein needed, or myeloma suspectedUACR and dipstick miss light chains Light chainsThe dipstick stays negative while the sulfosalicylic acid test is positive; urine electrophoresis shows an M-spike.Protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine
Most accurate GFR needed; amputee, cachexiaCreatinine unreliableInulin or iothalamate clearance; cystatin C

Pause point. The bait: a urine dipstick or a normal creatinine. The UACR catches the reversible stage, and hyperfiltration may keep the creatinine normal early.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: persistent albuminuria Ratio – UACR 30 mg/g or more · Persistence – 2 of 3 samples over 3 to 6 months · Exclude – exercise, fever, infection, heart failure, hyperglycemia

StageABIMeans

7Treatment
1

Every patientfrom diagnosis

Glycemic and blood pressure control; a statin from age 40 to 75
2

1st linepersistent albuminuria

ACE inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker), especially with BP over 130/80 In practiceIn practice: some guidance ties the ACE inhibitor or ARB to hypertension; a clinical reference starts it at the first albuminuria whatever the pressure.

Never both together; neither in pregnancy.

3

Addtype 2 diabetes, albuminuria persisting

SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitor if the eGFR is 20 or more

It also cuts hyperfiltration.

4

Foot ulcerneuropathic ulcer

Off-load the foot until it heals; inspection at each visit and podiatry
5

Referretinopathy moderate or worse

Ophthalmology: macular edema, any proliferative retinopathy, or nonproliferative that is moderate or worse
8Follow-up
Annual care
WhenDo
Type 2: at diagnosis, then yearlyDilated eye exam, UACR with creatinine, monofilament foot exam In practiceIn practice: after normal exams with well-controlled glycemia, every 1 to 2 years may be considered.
Type 1: within 5 years of onset, then yearlyFirst dilated eye exam
Type 1: from 5 years after diagnosis, then yearlyKidney screen
Every visitBlood pressure; inspect the feet once sensation is lost
A1c not at goal or after a therapy changeA1c every 3 months
A1c stable at goalA1c every 6 months
Age 19 to 49 with diabetes; every adult 50 or olderPneumococcal vaccine
Hypertension, kidney disease, lupus, sickle cell disease, nephrotoxic drugs or human immunodeficiency virus infectionKidney screen at diagnosis, then yearly or by risk
Routine visitsDepression screen; weight and tobacco counseling
Healthy adult without risk factorsNo kidney screen (USPSTF: insufficient evidence)
Practice
  1. 28-year-old woman had type 2 diabetes diagnosed 1 month ago Asymptomatic; walks daily and has cut out sugary drinks takes metformin; no other medical history BP 122/78 mm Hg · A1c 6.1% → Annual dilated eye exam → morbidity means the complications of diabetes, so the answer screens for one: the dilated eye exam finds retinopathy while it is still asymptomatic. Pneumococcal vaccination is indicated too, but it addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes; monthly A1c measures overlapping windows
  2. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years Due for his annual kidney screening; feels well takes metformin; no edema BP 128/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · A1c 7.4% → Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio → the most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold: the ratio detects 30 to 300 mg/g, the reversible stage. The dipstick stays negative until about 300 mg/day; a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection quantifies total protein when a non-albumin protein is suspected
  3. 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had a foot ulcer for 3 weeks painless plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head surrounding callus; foot warm and dry T 36.9 °C · pedal pulses normal · A1c 9.1% → Neuropathic ulcer → painless, plantar over a bony prominence and warm point away from arterial disease; normal pulses support a perfused foot, but neuropathy hides ischemic pain, so the ABI is still checked, and even a normal ABI and toe-brachial index only make arterial disease less likely; dry skin is autonomic denervation. Off-loading with a total contact cast is the single most important treatment, with debridement and glycemic control
  4. 56-year-old man has type 2 diabetes diagnosed today Thirst and frequent urination for 2 months no medical care in the past 10 years BP 134/84 mm Hg · A1c 8.2% · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → At diagnosis → in type 2 diabetes kidney screening starts at diagnosis and repeats yearly, because silent hyperglycemia predates the diagnosis by years; in type 1 it starts 5 years after diagnosis
  5. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 2 years asks about A1c frequency A1c at goal on her last three checks No change in her metformin dose for a year BP 118/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.4% → Check the A1c every 6 months → stable at goal means every 6 months; every 3 months is for an A1c not at goal or after a therapy change. Monthly values measure overlapping windows of the 90 to 120 day red cell lifespan
  6. 68-year-old man has had a painful ulcer at the toe tips for 1 month pain worse with the leg raised, better dangling cool pale foot; shiny, hairless skin T 36.8 °C · BP 148/86 mm Hg · absent pulses → Arterial ischemic ulcer → a painful ulcer at the toe tips on a cool, pale, pulseless foot is arterial: confirm with the ankle-brachial index. A neuropathic ulcer is painless and plantar on a warm foot; a venous ulcer is wet and sits at the medial malleolus
  7. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a single abnormal albumin-to-creatinine ratio ratio 64 mg/g on his annual screen Ran a 10K race the day before the sample BP 126/78 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Repeat the albumin-to-creatinine ratio → confirmation requires 2 of 3 abnormal samples over 3 to 6 months, which excludes transient albuminuria from exercise, fever, infection, heart failure or hyperglycemia; drug treatment starts once it persists
  8. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is due for vaccines Receives this season's influenza vaccine today no asplenia; no chronic lung or heart disease Does not smoke BP 120/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.8% → Pneumococcal vaccination → diabetes is a risk-based indication for pneumococcal vaccination in adults 19 to 49, and every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age; asplenia is not required
  9. 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years is seen for his annual foot exam ABI 1.5 in both legs radiograph shows calcified tibial arteries BP 138/80 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL → Noncompressible vessels → an index over 1.4 means calcified, noncompressible vessels, as in diabetes and end-stage renal disease; the next test is the toe-brachial index, abnormal at 0.7 or less, which can unmask arterial disease the ABI hides
  10. 24-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 Establishing care at a new clinic after a move uses an insulin pump; no kidney screening on record BP 112/70 mm Hg · A1c 7.3% → 5 years after diagnosis → in type 1 diabetes kidney screening starts 5 years after diagnosis, then yearly; it starts at diagnosis only in type 2, where hyperglycemia has been silent for years
  11. 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes asks what most reduces his risk of death smokes one pack of cigarettes daily Overdue for his eye and foot exams BP 136/84 mm Hg · A1c 7.0% → Smoking cessation → mortality means death, so choose the intervention with survival data: smoking cessation, then blood pressure control and a statin. The eye and foot exams prevent morbidity, not death
  12. 62-year-old woman has had a leg ulcer for 2 months shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus brown hemosiderin staining and ankle edema Mild ache, better with the leg raised T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal → Venous stasis ulcer → a shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus with hemosiderin and edema is venous stasis: duplex ultrasound, then compression
  13. 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 9 years albumin-to-creatinine ratio 85 mg/g second elevated value in 4 months; the first was 72 mg/g BP 134/82 mm Hg (similar at her last visit) · A1c 7.1% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → ACE inhibitor or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor → persistent albuminuria (2 of 3 samples elevated over 3 to 6 months) with a blood pressure above the American Diabetes Association target of under 130/80 mm Hg calls for an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and in type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 20 or more an SGLT2 inhibitor as well; a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL puts her eGFR well above 20. Together they are most likely to slow progression
  14. 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a foot ulcer that has not healed in 2 months plantar foot ulcer over a bony prominence; probe-to-bone test positive Foot radiograph normal T 37.2 °C · ESR 88 mm/h → Osteomyelitis → a probe that touches bone makes osteomyelitis likely, and an ESR over 70 supports it; plain films are insensitive early, so MRI comes next, then bone biopsy, which names the organism
  15. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes asks when to recheck her A1c A1c 9.4% after adding a second agent Takes metformin and sitagliptin; no low blood sugars BP 124/78 mm Hg · weight 82 kg → Check the A1c every 3 months → an A1c not at goal and a therapy change each mean every 3 months; every 6 months is for an A1c stable at goal
  16. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is enrolling in a drug study below-knee amputation of the right leg last year The study protocol needs an exact filtration rate before dosing BP 130/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL → Inulin or iothalamate clearance → measured clearance is the most accurate; creatinine is unreliable in amputees, cachexia, bodybuilders and cirrhosis, where cystatin C helps
  17. 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a warm, swollen, erythematous right foot swelling for 3 weeks no ulcer or break in the skin; no fever Cannot feel the monofilament on either foot T 36.9 °C · white cells 7,400/mm³ → Charcot arthropathy → a warm, swollen, red foot with no ulcer, fever or raised white count in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy suggests Charcot arthropathy (confirm with radiographs or MRI): immobilize; rocker-bottom deformity
  18. 32-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 26 Establishing care after a move; old records lost reports she has never had a dilated eye examination BP 116/72 mm Hg · A1c 7.6% → Within 5 years after diagnosis → in an adult with type 1 diabetes the first dilated eye exam comes within 5 years after onset, then yearly; in type 2 diabetes it comes at diagnosis. Retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced, so waiting for symptoms misses it
  19. 34-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging painful ulcer on her lower leg violaceous, undermined border grew from a small sore over 10 days Has inflammatory bowel disease with a recent flare T 37.3 °C · white cells 9,800/mm³ → Pyoderma gangrenosum → a rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border in inflammatory bowel disease or rheumatoid arthritis is pyoderma gangrenosum: biopsy and steroids, and never debride (pathergy)
  20. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has confirmed albuminuria ratio 140 mg/g, then 156 mg/g 3 months later Asks what most slows progression BP 138/86 mm Hg (similar at his last visit) · A1c 7.8% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → ACE inhibitor or ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor → with albuminuria and a blood pressure above the American Diabetes Association target of under 130/80 mm Hg, an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus, in type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 20 or more, an SGLT2 inhibitor slows progression; a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL puts his eGFR well above 20. Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB
  21. 66-year-old man has a chronic non-healing ulcer on his shin arose in an old burn scar 8 months ago rolled, everted edges No better despite compression and two courses of antibiotics T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal → Biopsy for Marjolin ulcer → an ulcer in a chronic wound or scar with rolled, everted edges that has not healed in over 3 months needs a biopsy for Marjolin ulcer
Management Neuropathic ulcer – off-loading (total contact cast) is the single most important intervention; debride callus and necrotic tissue; glycemic control · Infection – culture only if clinically infected, deep tissue rather than a swab · Perfusion – check the ABI anyway: mixed neuroischemic ulcers are common · Charcot arthropathy – warm, swollen, red foot with no ulcer, fever or raised white count in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy suggests it (confirm with radiographs or MRI): immobilize; rocker-bottom deformity
Why monthly A1c is wrong A1c reflects glycation across the 90 to 120 day red cell lifespan, so monthly values measure heavily overlapping windows; they add no information and prevent no complication. At goal, monthly testing is six times the 6-month schedule.
Two problems with the source explanation The source question for the first practice item (eye exam, pneumococcal vaccine or monthly A1c to prevent morbidity) came with two errors. 1. The pneumococcal rationale is wrong. It limited vaccination to patients over 65 or with asplenia, but every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age, and diabetes is itself a risk-based indication in adults 19 to 49, so she is a candidate. The eye exam wins because it targets a diabetes-specific complication; vaccination addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes. 2. The attribution is off. The annual bundle and A1c intervals come from the American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care, not the USPSTF.
Buzzword → Step 2 phrasing “Microalbuminuria” → “UACR 85 mg/g” · “hyperfiltration” → “creatinine 0.7” in a diabetic · “Kimmelstiel-Wilson” → “nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy” · “transient albuminuria” → “he ran a 10K yesterday.”
Transferable rule

Read the outcome noun before the options: morbidity, mortality, hospitalization and benefit are four different targets, and a distractor can be the right intervention for the wrong target. The most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold; the most specific or confirmatory test is the least likely to give a false positive. Risk factors set the prior probability and physical findings the posterior: when the exam contradicts the risk profile on three separate axes, rely on the exam.
